2500.tone: Cloarec-Heiss 1978: 'un système tonal à trois registres' for all eleven Banda varieties surveyed, Kpagua included; does not discuss stress/accent. Pan-Banda only (NOT Kpagua-specific; main data Togbo/Linda, though p. 5 fn. 1 folds 'la petite tribu des Pagwa des environs de Kouango' into the Yakpwa): Tisserant 1930, Essai sur la grammaire banda, pp. 23-24 'ACCENT' (PDF + scan in the copy consulted): 'La langue banda est chantée, c'est-à-dire, que chaque syllabe a sa tonalité propre... On distingue trois tons principaux... En dehors de l'accent de hauteur, il existe en banda un accent d'intensité qui affecte certaines syllabes des mots, en sorte que les syllabes non accentuées s'abrègent et ont une tendance à disparaitre: Béleda, tronc d'arbre, bleda; temô, marque du futur, tem; mar&, faire, mar' -- an intensity accent exists on 'certain syllables' but no placement rule is given (the three examples show pretonic/first-syllable and final-vowel reduction, no consistent position). Diki-Kidiri & Cloarec-Heiss 1985 (pan-Banda orthography, in the copy consulted): three level tones + two contour tones, no stress statement.

2502.dq: 1) O acento em Krenak é previsível na última sílaba do item lexical isolado; 2) O acento muda num domínio maior do que o da palavra lexical isolada, como a palavra ou frase fonológica.
2502.heavy: Not weight-sensitive by the author's explicit statement: 'não ser uma língua com sensibilidade ao peso silábico' (p. 198); 'a língua não apresenta sensibilidade ao peso, podendo, portanto, sílabas leves ou pesadas receberem proeminência' (p. 204).
2502.prule: Primary stress falls on the final syllable of the word (isolated lexical item) regardless of syllable weight: closed (C)VC finals, open V/CV finals and monosyllables (including monosyllabic grammatical morphemes) are all stressed. Author's metrical analysis: quantity-insensitive iambic feet built left to right, rightmost foot head = primary.
2502.srule: Secondary stress on the initial syllable of words of three or more syllables, in addition to the final primary stress; none in mono- and disyllables. Attested in 3- and 4-syllable words (exx. 357-365, e.g. [«ku.pa.»rak] 'onça', [«i.pç.k´dn.»tSa/] 'papagaio'); no medial rhythmic stresses are transcribed. Impressionistic (no acoustic study); Silva 1986 p. 56, quoted p. 198, hears it mainly as greater duration than the second syllable.
2502.quote: [p. 197] O acento em Krenak mostra-se como previsível, caindo sobre a última sílaba do item lexical isolado. 2502.idn: Krenak (língua Krenak), the surviving Botocudo/Borum variety; principal speaker Sebastiana de Souza (Ngut-krak), plus José Anato, Antônio Jorge and Jovelina at P. I. Vanuíre (the last two 'se consideravam Nakrehé'); data: Audio data recorded by Lucy Seki 1979-1982…
2502.exq_: [p. 190, Portuguese loans] Podemos concluir que palavras bissilábicas ou trissilábicas paroxítonas perdem a última sílaba átona e preservam a sílaba acentuada. Deste modo, a sílaba acentuada passa a ser a última da palavra, que recebe o acento primário, o que ocorre de acordo com o acento em Krenak.
2502.tone: No tone or pitch accent described; the prosodic chapter treats stress (acento) and intonation only (declarative falling F0, interrogative rising final syllable, pp. 202-203).
2502.exc_quote: [phrase-level; sec. 4.5.2.2 p. 201] No domínio da palavra fonológica ou frase fonológica, os acentos se reposicionam em Krenak, de modo que nem sempre uma palavra que costuma ser marcada com o acento primário (da sílaba final) no domínio lexical, na frase, receberá o acento no mesmo local. | [phrase-level; sec. 4.5.2.3 p. 205] d) Se ocorre um choque acentual, em posição não final de frase, o acento é relocado por meio da inversão iâmbica.
2502.sec_quote: [p. 198] Quando o item é formado por três sílabas, entretanto, um acento secundário é atribuído. Assim, aplica-se o acento primário na última sílaba, mas a primeira sílaba passa a receber um acento secundário. [p. 201] Porém, se tiver três ou mais sílabas, o acento primário será na última, mas o acento secundário marcará a primeira sílaba da palavra.

secx.sec_quote_tr: [p. 198] When the item consists of three syllables, however, a secondary stress is assigned. Thus the primary stress applies to the last syllable, but the first syllable comes to receive a secondary stress. [p. 201] But if it has three or more syllables, the primary stress will be on the last, while the secondary stress will mark the first syllable of the word.

2505.dflt: Citation form / phrase-final: penult primary in every word regardless of weight; secondary stress on even-numbered non-final syllables from the left (rhythmic lengthening), full grids 10 010 0110 01010 010110 0101010 01010110. 2505.prule: In words in isolation (= single-word phonological phrases, citation forms) and in phrase-final words, primary stress (head of the head foot = last foot of the word) is uniformly the penultimate syllable, 'regardless of vowel length' and 'regardless of the number of syllables in the word'; it carries the default High tone. The source derives this from a left-to-right iambic parse plus a ban on phrase-final long vowels (*V:]phi) that forces final trochaic reversal (two leftover short syllables form a final trochee; a single leftover final syllable is unparsed) and right-headedness. The source is explicit (§4.1) that this penult is the phrase-level only penult: in non-phrase-final words final shortening does not apply, the iambic parse can lengthen the word-final vowel, and 'the primary stress is penultimate in odd-parity words... and final in even-parity words' (with all-short vowels; a lexical long vowel restarts the count). The fixed and quantity-insensitive penult coding therefore holds for citation/phrase-final forms, which is what the source itself headlines ('default penultimate stress... left-to-right iambs with trochaic reversal, as in Kuikuro', §7).
2505.srule: Secondary (non-primary) stresses = heads of the non-final feet: left-to-right iambs lengthen and stress the even-numbered non-final vowels counted from the left edge, e.g. [(ala:)(makí:)lɨ] 's/he fell', [(tsiha:)(lama:)(kílɨ)] 'we fell'; a lexically long vowel (or a word-initial long vowel derived by fusion or initial-vowel deletion) always heads a foot and the iambic count restarts after it, so secondary placement is weight-sensitive. 2509.dloc: Ch. 6 'Akṣar-parivartan', section 'Balāghāt' (stress), pp. 187-188. Word-vs-sentence definition p. 187 top; sentence stress p. 188; 'Surāghāt' (pitch) pp. 188-189; stress-conditioned apheresis pp. 185-186.
2509.prule: fixed-second (quantity-insensitive): primary stress usually (prāyaḥ) on the second syllable of the word — the final syllable in disyllables, the middle syllable in trisyllables, the second syllable in longer words; monosyllables bear full stress in isolation; stress is non-contrastive ('nirarthak').
2509.srule: Secondary (gauṇ) stress on the first syllable of disyllables (primary on the second: śoṭhā'); in trisyllables secondary on the final syllable and tertiary on the first (primary on the middle: pāhuṇā hu > ṇā > pā). No secondary placement given for words of four or more syllables.
2509.quote: जहाँ तक अक्षर बलाघात का सम्बन्ध है, कुलुई में इसकी विभिन्न प्रवृत्तियाँ हैं। (1) एकाक्षरी शब्द सभी बलाघात्मक होते हैं, और इन में व्यंजन की अपेक्षा स्वर पर अधिक बल होता है—खा', पी', जा', आ'ण, शु'ण आदि। ... जब ये अकेले बोले जाएँ तो ये पूर्ण बलाघात हैं, वाक्य में प्रयोग होने से बलाघात बदल सकता है। (2) द्व्यक्षरी (disyllabic) शब्दों की स्थिति में प्रायः मुख्य (primary) बलाघात दूसरे अक्षर पर पड़ता है, तथा प्रथम अक्षर पर गौण (secondary) बलाघात रहता है। "शोठा" शब्द में 'ठा' पर मुख्य बल है और 'शो' पर गौण—शोठा'। इसी तरह कोठा', घाणी', काठू', शाब'र, लाब'र, बाणा', चोखा', चीक'र, ... नुहा'र, भाऊ', ... आदि।…

(3) तीन अक्षरों वाले शब्दों में प्रायः मध्य अक्षर पर मुख्य बलाघात होता है ... बहु-अक्षरी शब्दों में प्रायः दूसरे अक्षर पर मुख्य बलाघात रहता है ... …
2509.tone: Separate subsection 'Surāghāt' (pitch accent / 'tonic accent'), pp. 188-189: Thakur says Kului has no such clear and widespread use of tone as Chinese ('कुलुई में तान-सुर का इतना स्पष्ट और व्यापक प्रयोग तो नहीं, फिर भी इसके कई उदाहरण मिल जाते हैं'), but lists a handful of pairs distinguished by level vs (high-/low-)falling pitch: sān 'easy' vs 'favour', pūlā 'source list' vs 'grass shoe', ghaṛin 'stench' vs 'clod', seū 'apple' vs 'bridge', so 'that' vs 'sleep!', nī 'not' vs 'nineteen', hū̃ 'yes' with four pitch readings; a rising contour on the final word marks yes/no questions. He compares this to Karlgren's account of Chinese tones as residues of lost particles. Ranganatha 1980 (Kului chart p. 70: suprasegmentals = nasalisation + stress) and LSI-HP 2023 (Kulvi: nasalisation + length) do not list tone. A reviewer should weigh whether these pitch pairs (cf. the tone of neighbouring Kotgarhi/Koci from lost voiced aspirates, Hendriksen 1986) make Kului a marginal tone language; the stress rule itself is stated positionally and independently of pitch, so the record is coded on the stress statement with this caveat.

secx.sec_quote_tr: In disyllabic words the primary stress usually falls on the second syllable, and secondary stress remains on the first syllable. In the word śoṭhā the main force is on ṭhā and the secondary on śo ... (3) In three-syllable words the primary stress is usually on the middle syllable, secondary on the last and tertiary on the first. In the word pāhuṇā these stresses are on hu, ṇā and pā respectively.

tn.translation: In Kului the use of tone is not so clear and widespread [as in Chinese], yet several examples of it are found. ... The pitch contour is usually meaningful. If the word 'so' is on a level pitch its meaning is 'he/that', and if high-falling its meaning is 'go to sleep'. Likewise on level pitch 'nī' means 'not' and on high-falling it is 'nineteen'. Likewise take the word 'sān': if the tone is low falling its meaning is 'easy'; if on the contrary the tone is high falling its meaning is 'favour (ehsān)'.

2511.dq: अतः शब्द के उपान्त्य स्वर पर बलात्मक स्वराघात होता है चाहे वह ह्रस्व हो या दीर्घ। (p. 96: 'therefore the force stress falls on the penultimate vowel of the WORD, whether it is short or long'). p. 94 defines svarāghāt as emphasis on a particular vowel 'in a word at the time of pronunciation' (किसी शब्द में उच्चारण के समय किसी विशेष स्वर पर जोर देना) and sets sentence stress apart: 'कभी-कभी वाक्य म…
2511.dloc: Prastāvanā (introduction), section 'Svarāghāt', pp. 94-97; running text p. 96 (dagāṛā, dekhihāl) and conclusions 1, 2 (p. 96) and 5 (p. 97). archive.org, leaves n100-n101., adjective intensification (pp. 123-124) and permissive imperative (p. 145). Pandey 1977: 48.
2511.heavy: A full vowel, short or long ('चाहे वह ह्रस्व हो या दीर्घ'). The word-final vowel 'usually' becomes short and in speech 'usually' only ə remains ('अंतिम स्वर प्रायः ह्रस्व हो जाता है। बोलने में प्रायः उसके स्थान पर अ रह जाता है'), is 'half' ('आधी रह जाती है') or is lost ('कभी लुप्त भी हो जाती है'), and does not carry stress; the inherent -a of a consonant-final word counts as its final vowel (cf. Garhwali bald, conclusion 3: stress on ba 'because the final a is lost in speech').
2511.dflt: not applicable: every word has at least one full vowel; monosyllables (Pandey's bhol, khāl) stress their only vowel
2511.prule: Juyal 1967: 96-97 (Kumauni): the word-final vowel is usually shortened and in speech usually reduced to a (ə), left 'half' or lost, so force-stress falls on the penultimate vowel of the word, whether that vowel is short or long — bhitér, báiṇi, bhínā, bhúli, cáuṃṛo, cyā́lā (stress on e, ai, i, u, au, ā); dagā́ṛā (stress on gā), dekhihā́l (stress on hā: the inherent -a of a final consonant counts as the final vowel, cf. Garhwali bald, conclusion 3); an all-short three-vowel word stresses the middle vowel, khicáṛi (stress on ca; p. 97, conclusion 5). Over spoken syllables: the last syllable with a full vowel (penult in vowel-final words, final in consonant-final words). Emphatic adjectives (p. 96 conclusion 1; pp. 123-124: final vowel prolonged or stressed, or penultimate vowel stressed), the vocative singular (p. 120: penultimate vowel) and the permissive sense of the imperative (p. 145: final vowel) have their own stress placement.
2511.srule: Not mentioned in Juyal 1967, 'Svarāghāt', pp. 95-97 (the section describes a single force stress per word and never a second or rhythmic stress); also not mentioned in Pandey 1977: 47-48 or Kandpal 2012: 101-103.
2511.quote: शब्द दगाड़ा हो जाता है। भाषण में अंतिम आ कभी लुप्त भी हो जाती है। क्योंकि गा पर स्वराघात होता है। ... २—कुमाउँनी में ह्रस्वत्व की प्रवृत्ति अधिक है। अंतिम स्वर प्रायः ह्रस्व हो जाता है। बोलने में प्रायः उसके स्थान पर अ रह जाता है। अतः शब्द के उपान्त्य स्वर पर बलात्मक स्वराघात होता है चाहे वह ह्रस्व हो या दीर्घ। जैसे भितेर, बैंणि, भिना, भुलि, चौंड़ो, च्याला आदि शब्दों में अंतिम स्वर लिखा तो अवश्य जाता है किन्तु भाषण में स्वर ध्वनि आधी रह जाती है या अ हो जाती है फलस्वरूप उपान्तय स्वर क्रमशः ए, ऐ, इ, उ, औ, आ पर बलात्मक स्वराघात होता है। ... ५—कुमाउँनी में यदि तीन स्वर ध्वनियों का शब्द हो और तीनो…
2511.loc: Prastāvanā (introduction), section 'Svarāghāt', pp. 94-97; running text p. 96 (dagāṛā, dekhihāl) and conclusions 1, 2 (p. 96) and 5 (p. 97). archive.org, leaves n100-n101., adjective intensification (pp. 123-124) and permissive imperative (p. 145). Pandey 1977: 48.
2511.idn: Kumauni (कुमाउँनी) in general: the speech of Kumaon = hill parts of Almora, Pithoragarh and Nainital districts, from the eastern border of Garhwal to the Kali (Sharda) river; treated together with Garhwali as 'Madhya Pahāṛī'; no sub-dialect singled out in the stress section
2511.exq_: Conclusion 1, p. 96: 'गढ़वाली में कभी विशेषणों में गुणाधिक्य प्रगट करने के लिये उपान्त्य स्वर पर स्वराघात होता है जैसे मिट्ठो। यह प्रवृति कुमाउँनी में भी है।' Adjective intensification, pp. 123-124: 'किन्तु मध्य-पहाड़ी में व्रिशेषण शब्द के. अन्तिम स्वर को प्लुत कर देते हैं यदि अन्तिम ar gea [= स्वर…
2511.tone: No tone. Juyal (pp. 95-96) contrasts musical (gītātmak) accent, assigned to Vedic, with the dynamic (balātmak) accent of modern Indo-Aryan, weak in Hindi and Garhwali, stronger in Kumauni; Pandey 1977: 47-48 says the same (dynamic rather than musical accent) and adds that sentence pitch (sur) can change meaning ('इसके विपरीत सुर (पिच) के उतार चढ़ाव के कारण वाक्य में अर्थ परिवर्तन होता है').

2512.dq: L’accent porte généralement sur la syllabe initiale du radical des mots simples ou de chaque radical des composés, sauf si l’initiale du composé est un préfixe ou une forme courte assimilée à un préfixe.
2512.dloc: p. 204, sec. 3 'Particularités morphologiques', second paragraph (HAL deposit halshs-00006061 of the PUL chapter)
2512.prule: Root-initial stress: the accent falls on the initial syllable of the lexical root (radical) of a simple word; a prefix or a prefix-like reduced first member of a compound is never stressed (kâ-'raamwa, with the accent on the root thaamwa, vs 'thaamwa 'laeo); in compounds each root carries its own accent. Position is fixed relative to the root, not to the phonological word, so it is set by morphological structure (affix vs root), quantity-insensitive.
2512.srule: Simple words: not mentioned (Bril 2004, sec. 3 p.204, gives a single accent on the root-initial syllable and says nothing about secondary or rhythmic stress). Compounds: each radical carries an accent on its initial syllable, with no primary/secondary ranking ('thaamwa 'laeo, 'hâlûû 'bolaa, 'khuwo-'thaabwan); a prefix-like short first element is unaccented (kâ-'raamwa).
2512.quote: Voici d’abord quelques remarques sur l’accentuation des composés, puis un rappel sur les caractéristiques des diverses classes de noms, car celles-ci ont une influence sur la morphologie et les types de composés. L’accent porte généralement sur la syllabe initiale du radical des mots simples ou de chaque radical des composés, sauf si l’initiale du composé est un préfixe ou une forme courte assimilée à un préfixe. On oppose donc 'thaamwa 'laeo "femmes-esprits", qui a un accent sur chaque radical du composé, à kâ-'raamwa "génie féminin des airs", dont la syllabe initiale est la forme courte de …

2513.prule: Dynamic word stress (Druckakzent) on the first syllable of disyllables and trisyllables and on the antepenultimate syllable of words of four or more syllables, i.e. antepenultimate stress with initial stress as its short-word corollary; syllable-count only, no weight condition mentioned (syllabic nasals tn, glm in verbs count as syllables). Bergmann frames it as 'no binding rule' but 'rules that hold almost without exception' (usually/normally on the first syllable; a few exceptions such as porá). Pfantz 2005 independently gives initial stress in 2-3-syllable words (very few exceptions) and 'the third syllable' for 4+-syllable words.
2513.srule: Exists, placement not given: 'in very long words there may be, beside the main accent, one or more secondary accents (Nebenakzente) in the same word' -- no positions or examples are given. 2513.tone: Bergmann 1966:19 says high and low tone were repeatedly suspected but could not be proven and concludes the contrasts are vowel length, not pitch (duu 'straight' vs du 'dumb, deaf'; muundi- vs mundi-; kooro vs koro), while noting some speakers' marked sentence melody. Pfantz & Pfantz 2005:22 report second-hand that Hardie (2003:63-92) 'identifies a distinction between falling and non-falling tone on Kuman words' with only a few minimal pairs (tone unwritten) and deny any vowel- or consonant-length contrast, i.e. the two sources disagree on what the marginal contrast is (length vs word tone). Hardie 2003 (MA thesis, ANU, 'Is Kuman tonal?') is not open and was not seen; if it establishes lexical tone proper the record could move to tone or pitch accent with a stress statement. Both first-hand sources nevertheless describe stress in the same syllable-counting terms.

2515.dq: Kapitonov p.33: 'the most robust pattern is for the primary stress to fall on the penultimate syllable, if the word is longer than one syllable. In monosyllables the stress will fall on the only syllable.' Coleman 1982 p.21: 'Word-level stress is linguistically significant in Gunbarlang because it serves to mark word-boundaries.'
2515.dloc: Kapitonov 2019, ch. 2 Phonology, sec. 2.6 'Stress', pp. 32-35 (quotes from pp. 33, 34, 35). Coleman 1982, sec. 1.10 'Word-level stress', thesis pp. 21-24.
2515.heavy: Not weight-conditioned. Kapitonov p.35: 'The antepenultimate stress, as in (2.20a), does not systematically originate in stress shifting off from a light syllable. Example (2.22) shows that it does not have to even when the next one left is potentially heavier (CVC vs. CV): kaddà-karrmíli'.
2515.prule: Author's stated analysis: primary stress is 'fixed lexical, with a tendency towards penultimate' -- every morpheme is inherently specified for stress location (or for no stress); stems take precedence over affixes (stem gets primary, affixes secondary; a stem with no stress specification lets a prefix carry the primary). Surface pattern: the most robust/frequent locus is the penultimate syllable of the word (monosyllables stressed on their only syllable), but in verbs primary stress falls frequently on the pronominal prefix, on the antepenult, or on the final syllable, and this is not weight-driven. Stress is not contrastive; cued by higher pitch and greater intensity, not vowel length. Coleman 1982 p.21 states a plain penultimate rule ('a rise in pitch and an increase in duration of the vowel in the penultimate syllable in a word'), no stress on monosyllables, with perturbations from intramorphemic elision (stress 'moved back'), reduplication (first syllable of each copy stressed) and stressed first syllables of polysyllabic argument prefixes in long verbs.
2515.srule: Secondary stress 'tends to go leftwards on alternating syllables from wherever the primary stress is placed... but in longer words gaps get larger' (ngà-bak-rdúkkume, kaddà-karrmíli; kàdda-nganj-kánginj, ngàdda-makàrninjdjánganj); no word has more than three audible stresses; clash with the primary is rare but possible (man-rdawùrrng-búrrinj); affixes take secondary stress when the stem carries the primary; the author sees no 'systematically organised metrical structure' in this variation. Earlier, Coleman 1982:21: a single secondary stress 'on the third preceding syllable, or fifth syllable from the end of the word' before the penultimate primary, with a lesser pitch rise and smaller lengthening; in 7+ syllable words the syllables before it are 'run together'.

2527.prule: Stress falls on the heavy syllable (bimoraic rime: VC or V:). Every simple lexical word is /#(CV)ˈCVC#/ or /#(CV)ˈCV:#/: exactly one stressed heavy syllable, which is word-final, optionally preceded by one unstressed light (monomoraic CV) syllable; every simple grammatical word surfaces as a single stressed heavy syllable. Stress is therefore predictable from syllable weight and non-contrastive (Angenot-de Lima & Angenot 2000: 157). Extensionally identical to fixed final stress for simple words (max. 2 syllables).

Simple words are at most disyllabic; no secondary or rhythmic stress is described.

2528.prule: Word stress is predictable and falls on the final (main) syllable: a phonological word is one stressed syllable optionally preceded by one unstressed presyllable (with reduced [ə]); monosyllables are stressed, disyllables are stressed on the final syllable (WS). Words never exceed two phonetic syllables.
2528.srule: None within the word: 'So the Stress pattern is only the strong stress on the main syllable' (words are at most presyllable + stressed main syllable). A weaker secondary stress is described only on the non-final word(s) of Rhythm Groups (reduplications and compounds), whose last word carries the primary stress.

2528.tone: No lexical tone. 'Pitch in Kuay is conditioned by the structure of the syllable... There are three pitches: High, Mid-High and Low; and they are all predictable.' (p. 20, sec. 3.4); 'Pitch on initial unstressed syllables is always low.' (p. 23, sec. 3.4.4).
